In controlled tests (including a televised one where flags of different colors were waved identically), bulls charged all flags equally when they moved, and ignored all of them when still — including a stationary person dressed in red standing in the ring.

**What actually provokes the charge:** Motion. The bullfight's cape is dangerous because the matador *waves* it. Bulls, like many prey-and-predator animals, react to movement as threat or challenge, and a fighting bull has additionally been bred and provoked into aggression. The cape's red is tradition and showmanship — with a practical footnote: red hides bloodstains from the crowd.

**The right model:** Bulls charge at movement and provocation, not color; they literally cannot see the color in question. Keep the red shirt. The farm rule worth teaching instead: don't run, wave, or startle — it's what you *do*, not what you wear.
A housefly just landed on my lunch for the third day running — possibly the same one? My brother says houseflies only live 24 hours, so it can't be. Who's right?

You might well be looking at the same fly. Your brother has confused the housefly with a different insect entirely.

**The wrong model:** The housefly lives a single day — hatches, buzzes, dies — making every fly a stranger.

**The observation it can't explain:** The housefly's own life cycle doesn't fit in 24 hours. Just the developmental stages — egg (about a day), larva/maggot (several days), pupa (several more days) — take over a week before an adult fly even exists. An adult that then died in a day would make the species' whole schedule absurd, and laboratory colonies of houseflies are routinely kept for weeks. The real figures: adult houseflies live roughly 15–30 days, longer in cool conditions, shorter in the thick of summer activity.

**Where the 24 hours belongs:** The mayfly. Adult mayflies famously live from a few hours to a day or two — some species' adults don't even have functional mouths, since eating isn't part of their one-day reproductive mission. 'The insect that lives a day' is a true fact pinned to the wrong insect, the way many animal myths work.

**The right model:** Your lunch visitor can plausibly be a repeat guest for two to four weeks — the same individual, learning nothing about your feelings on the matter. The correct response is a food cover, not a eulogy. Your brother owes the fly an apology for the premature obituary.
We found a baby bird on the ground and my kids want to put it back in the nest, but I was raised on "never touch a baby bird — the mother will smell you and abandon it." Were we wrong to hesitate?

You were wrong to hesitate, but in the gentlest possible way — the myth is false, and acting on the truth quickly is exactly right.

**The wrong model:** Birds navigate motherhood by smell: touch the chick and your human scent marks it as foreign, so the mother rejects it.

**The observation it can't explain:** Most birds have a poor sense of smell — it's one of their weakest senses (vultures and kiwis are famous exceptions). A mother bird generally *cannot* smell you on her chick, and wildlife rehabilitators return handled chicks to nests routinely; the parents resume feeding them without hesitation. The abandonment the myth predicts essentially doesn't happen from touch. If it did, bird banding — where researchers handle nestlings constantly to ring them — would be a conservation catastrophe instead of a standard tool.

**The right model, with the important nuance:** Put the chick back — promptly, gently, in the nearest nest or sheltered spot. Two honest caveats: first, if the 'baby' is a *fledgling* — feathered, hopping, parents nearby scolding you — it isn't lost; it's in flight school, and the kindest act is to leave it and keep pets away. Second, the real dangers to a handled chick are chilling and delay, not scent. So the old warning had the right instinct (don't interfere casually) attached to the wrong mechanism, which made people hesitate in the one case where quick hands help. Touch, return, wash your hands, watch from a distance: the mother will do the rest.
In college we joked that "every drink kills a million brain cells." I assume that's exaggerated, but is it basically true — does alcohol kill brain cells?

It's exaggerated past the point of being true — but what alcohol actually does is more specific and, in its own way, more worth knowing.

**The wrong model:** Each drink destroys a batch of neurons, permanently subtracting from a fixed lifetime supply — brain damage as simple arithmetic, one beer at a time.

**The observation it can't explain:** Studies comparing the brains of heavy drinkers and non-drinkers found no significant difference in neuron *count*. If routine drinking killed neurons wholesale, the cell counts would diverge measurably — they don't. Even in severe alcoholism, the classic brain shrinkage visible on scans is largely loss of *volume* in the connections and white matter, and it partially reverses with sustained abstinence. Dead neurons don't come back; this damage partly does, so most of it can't be cell death.

**What alcohol actually does:** It damages the *dendrites* — the branching connections neurons use to communicate — and disrupts signaling, which degrades function without killing the cell. Think less 'demolition' and more 'corroded wiring'. The serious exceptions are real, though: binge drinking can injure neurons in vulnerable regions, chronic abuse plus thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome with genuine, permanent neuron loss, and the developing brain (fetus, adolescent) is far more vulnerable than the adult one.

**The right model:** Alcohol mostly impairs and, with heavy use, injures the brain's *connections* — much of it recoverable — rather than mowing down brain cells drink by drink. The college joke is wrong as arithmetic. The honest version is less quotable but more useful: you don't lose the hardware count; you degrade the network, and the network can heal if the insult stops.
My fitness tracker nags me to drink 8 glasses of water a day. Is the "8×8 rule" real science or folklore?

Folklore wearing a lab coat — and the real science is more reassuring.

**The wrong model:** Every human needs eight 8-ounce glasses (about 1.9 liters) of *water* daily, as a fixed prescription, separate from other drinks and food.

**The observation it can't explain:** Nobody can find the rule's source. A 2002 review by physiologist Heinz Valtin searched the literature and found no study establishing 8×8 for healthy adults in temperate climates. The likely ancestor is a 1945 Food and Nutrition Board note recommending about 2.5 liters of water daily — *from all sources, including food* — whose second half got dropped in retelling. Meanwhile the rule's universality fails on contact with reality: a small sedentary person in a cool climate and a large athlete in August cannot share one number, and about 20–30% of daily water normally arrives in food (fruit, rice, even bread is over a third water). Coffee and tea count too — their mild diuretic effect doesn't cancel their water content.

**The right model:** For healthy adults, thirst is a well-calibrated instrument — drink to thirst, drink with meals, and drink more with heat, exercise, illness, or age (older adults' thirst signals blunt, so they warrant deliberate attention). Pale-yellow urine is the practical gauge. Genuinely forcing water beyond thirst has its own risk — endurance athletes have died of *over*hydration (hyponatremia), something no one has ever done from drinking to thirst.

Your tracker isn't giving you science; it's giving you a memorable number. The science says the number is personal, and your body already computes it.
My roommate won't stand in front of the microwave while it runs and says microwaved food is "a little bit radioactive." I say he's confusing things. Settle it.

You're right, and the confusion has a precise location: the word 'radiation' covers two opposite things, and your roommate is treating them as one.

**The wrong model:** Radiation is radiation — microwaves irradiate food the way nuclear material irradiates its surroundings, leaving the food faintly radioactive.

**The observation it can't explain:** Radioactivity means unstable atoms spitting out particles and changing into other elements. For radiation to *make* something radioactive or damage molecules by ionization, its photons need enough energy to knock electrons off atoms. Microwave photons are nowhere close — they're roughly a hundred thousand times too weak. They sit on the electromagnetic spectrum down by radio waves, far below visible light, let alone X-rays. A photon of ordinary light carries more energy than a microwave photon, and nobody worries that a salad left under a lamp becomes radioactive. Microwaved food also shows no residual energy of any kind: the moment the oven stops, the microwaves are gone — they were never stored, only absorbed as heat.

**The right model:** Microwaves heat by *agitation*, not ionization: the oscillating field makes water molecules in the food rotate back and forth, and the friction of billions of molecules jiggling is the heat. It's cooking, mechanically similar to rubbing your hands together. The oven's shielding and door mesh exist because leaking microwaves could heat *you* the same way they heat soup — a burn concern, not a radiation-poisoning one, and the interlock shuts the magnetron when the door opens anyway. Your roommate can stand where he likes, but his food is no more radioactive than toast.
In our house the five-second rule is basically law: food dropped on the floor is fine if you grab it fast. Please tell me science backs us up. My germophobe sister says it doesn't.

Your sister wins this one, and the experiment that settles it is almost cruelly simple.

**The wrong model:** Bacteria need time to climb aboard — there's a grace period, roughly five seconds, during which dropped food stays clean.

**The observation it can't explain:** When researchers dropped food onto bacteria-contaminated surfaces and tested it after different contact times — under a second, five seconds, thirty, a minute — bacteria were on the food at *every* interval, including the shortest. Transfer begins on contact; there is no grace period for bacteria to pack their bags. What actually determined contamination wasn't the clock but the food and the floor: wet foods (watermelon was the worst in the studies) pick up far more bacteria than dry ones, because moisture is the transfer highway, and smooth tile transfers more than carpet. Time did matter at the margins — longer contact, somewhat more bacteria — but the difference between one second and five was never 'safe versus unsafe'.

**The right model:** The moment food touches the floor, assume it has whatever the floor has. The real questions are how clean the floor is, how wet the food is, and who's eating it (a healthy adult and an immunocompromised toddler are different risk calculations). Your house rule isn't science — it's a family treaty about acceptable risk, which is a fine thing to have as long as everyone knows it's a treaty. The five seconds were never doing anything except ending arguments. Your sister should get to say she told you so exactly once.

A roulette player next to me said "red has come up ten times in a row, so black is due — the odds have to even out." I know this is called the gambler's fallacy, but I couldn't explain *why* it's wrong in a way that convinced him. Help.

Here's the explanation that usually lands, because it uses his own intuition against the fallacy.

**The wrong model:** Randomness has a memory and a conscience — the wheel 'owes' balance, so a streak of red creates a debt that black must repay soon.

**The observation it can't explain:** Ask him what physical mechanism would do the remembering. The wheel has no record of the last ten spins; the ball doesn't know. Each spin, red and black (18 pockets each on a European wheel) have exactly the same probability as every other spin — 18/37 — no matter what history preceded it. And here's the deeper point his intuition is mangling: the law of large numbers does say proportions even out over time — but they even out by *dilution*, not by *correction*. After ten reds, the next ten thousand spins will be roughly half black, and that flood of ordinary results makes the original streak a rounding error. The universe never pays the debt; it just buries it.

**The check that exposes it:** If 'black is due' were true after ten reds, it must also be true that the wheel becomes *less* likely to show red the longer the streak runs — which means a streak could never reach eleven, twelve, twenty. But streaks of twenty happen regularly in casinos, on schedule, exactly as often as memoryless probability predicts. The fallacy forecasts a force that would prevent the very streaks that trigger it.

**The right model:** Independent events don't compensate; they accumulate. The wheel isn't a friend keeping score — it's a machine with no past. The casino doesn't need the fallacy to be false in the long run, either: it profits from the house edge on every spin, streak or no streak.

My personality quiz says I'm "left-brained" — logical, not creative — because I'm an accountant. My sister the artist is "right-brained." Is there real neuroscience behind this or is it astrology with a lab coat?

Mostly astrology with a lab coat — but it's built around a real piece of neuroscience, which is why it survives. Here's the separation.

**The wrong model:** People come in two cognitive types, dominated by one hemisphere: the left (logic, language, analysis) or the right (creativity, intuition, art), and your personality is your dominant side.

**The observation it can't explain:** Brain imaging of actual people doing actual tasks. A large study of over 1,000 brains looked for individuals whose networks were consistently stronger on one side — the 'dominance' the quiz requires — and didn't find them. Everyone uses both hemispheres constantly, joined by a massive data cable (the corpus callosum, ~200 million fibers). And the functions refuse to stay in their assigned boxes: language is left-dominant in most people, yet the right hemisphere handles its tone, humor, and context; mathematics recruits both sides; and creativity — the supposed right-brain monopoly — lights up distributed networks across the whole brain in every study of it.

**The true kernel:** Lateralization is real at the level of *functions*, not *people*. Split-brain patients (whose corpus callosum was cut to treat epilepsy) showed that each hemisphere has genuine specializations — the left typically leads speech production, the right leads certain spatial and face-processing tasks. That Nobel-worthy science got inflated by pop psychology into a personality typology it never supported.

**The right model:** You are not a left-brain person; you are a whole-brain person whose *tasks* lean on different networks at different moments — including when you, the accountant, spot the elegant pattern in a spreadsheet, which is as creative an act as your sister's brushwork. The quiz measured your job description, not your hemispheres.
Everyone says Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth. My geography-nerd friend says "it depends what you mean by tallest." Is he just being pedantic?

He's being precise, and in this case precision changes the answer — Everest holds only one of the three titles.

**The wrong model:** 'Tallest mountain' is a single obvious ranking, and Everest tops it, full stop.

**The observations it can't explain:** Tallest *from where, to where*? Everest's summit is the highest point above sea level: 8,849 meters. But measure from base to peak and the winner is Mauna Kea in Hawaii — about 10,210 meters from its base on the ocean floor to its summit, more than a kilometer 'taller' than Everest; most of it is simply underwater. Measure differently again — farthest from Earth's center — and the winner is Chimborazo in Ecuador: because Earth bulges at the equator, Chimborazo's summit sits about 2 kilometers farther from the planet's center than Everest's does, despite being over 2,600 meters lower above sea level. Three measurements, three champions, all correct.

**The right model:** Everest's title is 'highest elevation above sea level' — which is a genuinely meaningful title, since sea level is the shared reference for altitude, weather, and the thin air that makes Everest lethal. But it's a *convention*, not a law of nature. The pedantry dissolves once you see that 'tallest' was never one question. Your friend isn't quibbling with Everest's record; he's pointing out the record book has three pages. The honest sentence is: Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, Mauna Kea is the tallest from base to summit, and Chimborazo's peak is the farthest point from Earth's center — and each fact is more interesting than the slogan.
My trivia team argued about the largest desert on Earth. Half of us said the Sahara. The quizmaster said Antarctica. That feels like a trick. Is it?

It's a trick only if you think 'desert' means 'hot sand' — and unlearning that is the entire point of the question.

**The wrong model:** A desert is a landscape of dunes and cacti: heat is part of the definition.

**The observation it can't explain:** The technical definition of a desert is about *precipitation*, not temperature: a region receiving very little precipitation (commonly under 250 mm a year). By that measure, Antarctica qualifies overwhelmingly — its interior receives as little as 20–50 mm of precipitation a year, less than much of the Sahara, making it the largest desert on Earth at about 14.2 million km², comfortably bigger than the Sahara's ~9.2 million. The Arctic basin qualifies too. All that Antarctic ice doesn't contradict the classification; the ice accumulated over millions of years precisely because what little snow falls almost never melts or leaves. A place can be covered in frozen water and still be one of the driest places on the planet — the water is locked up, not delivered.

**The right model:** Deserts are defined by water *income*, not by temperature or scenery: hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian), coastal deserts (Atacama, driest of all), and polar deserts (Antarctica, the Arctic). The Sahara keeps its title as the largest *hot* desert — your half of the team wasn't wrong about the fact, just about the category. The quizmaster's answer is correct, and now you know the definition that makes it correct instead of merely clever: a desert is where water rarely arrives, whatever the thermometer says.
